subject: Banking
title: Danske Bank's $230 Billion Scandal
description: A fast breakdown of Danske Bank's $230 Billion Scandal for builders.

hook.text: $230 billion in suspicious money flowed through Danske Bank's Estonian branch.

buildup.text: From 2007 to 2015, Danske Bank's tiny Estonian branch processed transactions from Russian oligarchs and shell companies.

discovery.text: A single whistleblower, Howard Wilkinson, reported the suspicious flows. Management dismissed his concerns for years.

twist.text: Danske Bank's CEO resigned, its stock dropped 50%, and Denmark's reputation as a clean financial center was destroyed.

climax.text: A small branch in Estonia laundered more money than Denmark's entire GDP.

punchline.text: $230 billion laundered. One whistleblower. Years of ignored warnings.

quiz.question: How much suspicious money flowed through Danske Bank's Estonian branch?

details.summary: Danske Bank's Estonian branch processed over $230 billion in suspicious transactions from Russia and former Soviet states between 2007 and 2015, making it one of the largest money laundering scandals in history.
details.whyItMatters: The Danske scandal showed that even in well-regulated Europe, a small branch of a major bank could launder hundreds of billions essentially unchecked for nearly a decade.
takeaways: Over $230 billion flowed through a tiny Estonian branch
Most funds originated from Russia and former Soviet countries
Internal whistleblowers were ignored for years before exposure

faq.question: How did $230 billion flow through undetected?
faq.answer: The Estonian branch operated with minimal oversight from Copenhagen headquarters. Non-resident accounts were processed through a separate IT system that bypassed standard compliance monitoring tools.

faq.question: What happened to Danske Bank after the scandal?
faq.answer: The CEO resigned, the stock price collapsed, and the bank faced criminal investigations in multiple countries. Danske agreed to forfeit $2 billion in a US settlement and remains under investigation in Denmark and Estonia.
